# Scoring guide 

### Content

- Getting the right answer is only a small part of the grade
- Good quality interpretation of your results is the name of the game
- If you see something that looks unusual in your data (outlier, some unusual distribution type) - investigate it! 
- When explaining your results, say something interesting about them. Did it match your expectations? Why or why not? 
- Brief explanations that simply repeat what I can visually see myself will not receive a good score
- On the other hand, filling the homework with parag raphs of not very interesting description is not valuable either. The goal isn't to write the most words, but find the most interesting things in the data.
- You do not need to be an expert in movies to get a good grade on this assignment, but I will expect you to look up basic information, such as what does `vote_average` mean and so on to help you understand and set expectations your data.
- The information requested in the question prompts are only a starting point, if you find other interesting information along the way, please report that. You don't need to look at the data forever but if there is obviously something else interesting in the data you should report it.
- You must have up to Question 1 completed for the homework preliminary check on Thursday, September 3

### Technical

- Make sure your graphs are produced using `ggplot()`, are well labeled, and are easy to read. Using `ggplot()` is a requirement.
- Make sure your tables are produced with the `kable()` function from the `knitr` package, are well labeled, and are easy to read. You can make your tables prettier with the `kableExtra` package. Using `kable()` is a requirement.
- Make sure you do not have anything rendered in your HTML file besides your results and, when asked for by a question, your code. That means no warnings, messages, or other unnecessary output should appear in your final rendered HTML file.

# Questions

## Question 1: Displaying and describing the data (25 points)

For this investigation, we are going to examine movie runtime length. 

### 1a. Investigating `runtime`

Using the Think-Show-Tell framework from the textbook, investigate the distribution of `runtime`.

> Think

> Show

*For this section, please make an appropriate graph or table and briefly describe what you observe*

> Tell

*Please interpret the meaning of your finding here, especially with respect to your expectation*

### 1b. Investigating `runtime` by genre type

Using the Think-Show-Tell framework from the textbook (example on page 71), investigate the distribution of `runtime` but you should compare the differences between these three genres: `Action`, `Comedy`, and `Drama`. You should count a movie as being part of the genre if the column `genres` contains one of the three types listed here. It may help you to make a new column that is called `key_genre` and so on using the `mutate()` and `case_when()` verbs from `dplyr()`. Make note of any differences between the three and think about why, if there are differences, why they would exist.

> Think

> Show

> Tell

### 1c. Thinking about your results

Consider the results of 1a. and 1b. together. What can we understand about how different movie types affect the distribution of `runtime`?

## Question 2: Comparing groups (25 points)

One interesting question is whether movies that are made in multiple countries are in some way different than movies that are made solely in the United States. 

### 2a. Compare production location vs. genre

Make a contingency table to compare the number of movies made solely in the United States by the three major genre types - `Action`, `Comedy`, and `Drama`

*Hint*: You can use the `dplyr` verb `ifelse` to make a new column as to whether the movies are produced solely in the United States. A movie that is made in multiple countries should be considered to fail this condition.

## Question 3: Considering deviations (20 points)

### 3a. Selecting your data

Make a subset of `genres` by selecting any genre outside of the three most common types (but should still be present in at least 10 movies) by using the `filter` verb.

### 3b. Finding the average

Make a table of the averages of `vote_average`, `revenue`, `runtime`, and `budget`. Show your code using the `#| echo: true` code block option. 

### 3c. Normalizing the data

Add a row to your table; find how many $z$ units each of your selected genre's averages are away from the overall averages in the dataset. Show your code using the `#| echo: true` code block option. 

### 3d. Thinking about your results

Interpret your results - what do the $z$ scores indicate about how similar the subset is to the overall dataset? Are the results surprising to you? What are the limitations of your findings? What can you say about the genre after reviewing this table?

## Question 4: Your own investigation (20 points)

Similar to the previous questions, think of your own question that you would like to ask of the data, ideally one that goes deeper into one of the questions considered above. The best way to approach this question is to think about what would be interesting to know or maybe something where you have an expectation about something in the data that you can test by viewing the distributions of the variables or by comparing categorical variables. Use the Think-Show-Tell procedure to conduct your investigation. Think deeply about what your result means. 

You will be graded on whether you are asking an interesting and meaningful question, the appropriateness of the statistical technique used to analyze the question, and how you interpret the result.
